utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Exhibit number D281. Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I know Your Honour will have found Blace and the Djeneral Jankovic crossing on page 16 of the atlas Exhibit 83, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have only a limited number of questions to ask you, Dr. Aleksovski, but let me see if I understand your evidence a little bit first. Where you say there was one person who spoke to you of the reason for leaving Kosovo, are you able to identify that person by reference number or indeed by name in the exhibits you've produced?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a person who was standing in line to be examined. At that moment, the person had not yet been identified. And if I saw him or her today, I wouldn't be able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise the other people who you say were spoken of by your staff giving this as the explanation, are you able to identify any of them by name or by reference number in your exhibits? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which are the individuals who gave this account that you can identify for me, who gave this explanation for leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you'd better identify the explanation, because there are two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The explanation for leaving because of the NATO bombs. Can you point to the individuals by name, in private session, or by number in your exhibit so I can know who they are?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I heard one such person giving that explanation, but the person's turn for examination had not yet come, and by that time he hadn't yet been received, and we hadn't gotten his name down. So if we had known in advance that you would be asking this question, that there would be this entire procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line of questioning. I'll move on to something else. You as the chief did not go out and talk to the refugees. That's one of the things you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I did talk to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't go out routinely. You didn't go out regularly and speak to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It was not primarily my job to go out and talk to refugees, but in passing, yes, I came into contact with some of them and talked to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your teams only went out and responded to requests for medical assistance. You didn't examine -- your teams didn't examine every incoming refugee as a matter of routine.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They examined only those people who wanted to be examined. They would come to the tent, be examined, and leave. We didn't even -- we didn't need to examine all the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your records only cover the period 25th of March or 24th of March until the end of April?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your last answers before the refreshment break, Dr. Aleksovski, where you gave a lot of statistics, you said related to the period 25th to the 27th. Now, that was the 25th to the 27th of which month?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our activity began on the 24th without any interventions involved. On the 25th March we started actually working with patients, until the 27th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So this covers the whole period. In that -- very well. It was a matter of clarity, and thank you for that. Obviously -- how many medical staff did you have altogether?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the emergency service, until the 6th of May, there were four medical teams, three at Gornje Blace, one at Donje Blace. On the 6th when they moved to the Stenkovac 1 refugee camp, there were three medical emergency teams and one team supplied by the health centre in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were simply in no position to service the medical needs of 300, 350.000 people, obviously.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did cover all their requests. We met all their requests. It was only later that some other humanitarian organisations arrived, and we referred milder cases to them, but all the serious cases went through the emergency medical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The medical conditions and the humanitarian conditions in the Macedonian camps were subject of widespread international comment and some criticism; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the foreign media reported this, but I know that at the end when all the impressions and reports were pulled I can say that our emergency medical service was praised by our trade union for dealing with the job with flying colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a river bordering one of the camps?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was a river that was close to the temporary admission camp, the Lepenac River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the Croatian Red Cross, to your recollection, record bodies being deposited in that river? Do you remember that as a public report?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of any bodies. I heard that pistols had been thrown into that river, but there was no official confirmation of that. I personally didn't see it, but people talked about it a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look at three contemporary news photographs and see if you'd like to comment on them, please. Do you read and speak English, Dr. Aleksovski, or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first photograph has the caption -- has the dateline 1999 and simply reads: "A distressed mother with her daughter are prevented by Macedonian soldiers from leaving Blace camp." Does the photograph there fit with your recollection of circumstances at Blace?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph is marked as being taken in 1999, but it doesn't say where it was taken. Clarify, if you will, because I haven't seen a scene like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The caption says: "A distressed mother with her daughter are prevented by Macedonian soldiers from leaving Blace camp." Does this accord with your recollection of circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was Blace was of the camps that you went to, Doctor? Doctor, did you hear the question? Did you go to Blace camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you answer the question asked by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see Blace on page 16, east of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I will answer. Crowds such as this one in the picture were there. It is the true the police prevented them from entering town because I told you what would have happened if such a crowd of people rushed into the town uncontrollably. I can't say I saw this exact scene, but it's true they were not allowed from going further, from leaving, because at the time the camps were being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph is titled: "A distressed Kosovar Albanian woman in the chaos of fifty thousand refugees living in the increasingly overcrowded Blace camp." It just says 1999, it doesn't give the month. Does this again accord in general with your recollection of Blace camp's conditions?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat: That picture is very clear in my memory. Wherever I went, I saw all kinds of scenes, but I can say also that there were scenes that had been stage managed. You now made me say something that I didn't want to say as a medical professional, but maybe you will see and hear more of my colleagues who will tell you the same thing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There were pictures that were set up, scenes that were rigged, and we were able to see how they were propping an alleged wounded person so that they could be photographed, and the photograph was presented the same day. So this particular picture could be a reflection of something that was the truly happened but it could also be stage managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, look at the next one, then, please. There are the police there -- or, rather, the Macedonian soldiers. Would they be willing to be stage managed on behalf of the photographer, or were they doing what they normally did?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the army personnel did this at the border crossing. This was done by the police. You know, when someone sees a camera there, they become curious and perhaps pose for the photographer. Perhaps there was a crowd there. Perhaps some of them were queueing in line to get to the city as soon as possible and were prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, I cannot interpret this photograph. I can just tell you that I see a crowd in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to consider part of the contents of some five reports on what happened at the Macedonian border, and I'm going to try and do it swiftly. Before I do, have I got your evidence correct to this extent, that in the first few days at the end of March the flow of refugees was small, low in number?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was in that early period of time that you say the explanation for the refugees being there was the NATO bombing? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my presence, as I have explained to you, one woman said that, and I heard from other colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Aleksovski, don't repeat everything. We just don't have time in this court. Was it right that the explanation coming from the woman and from your colleagues about NATO bombings was in the early days, that is, the last days of March?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later --

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25th, 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later when the flow of refugees went up and was of course in the thousands so there would be 300.000 there eventually, or 400.000, whatever it was, the explanation came of ethnic cleansing; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Later on in Stenkovac 2, everyone said that they were fleeing from the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, first on the overhead projector because it's in English, at a document headed "Medical Group." While this is coming, are you aware of an organisation called Physicians for Human Rights, a Nobel Peace Prize winning organisation, visiting Kosovo Albanian refugees in your camps?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's what it is. We called them Doctors Without Borders. I don't know if it's the same organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... another organisation. Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the report could go on the overhead projector, I'll read just a few passages of it, sufficient, I hope, to make the points I wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a report released on April the 4th of 1999, so fairly early, and the report concluded that at that stage the risks of death and disease were growing exponentially worse day by day, with people collapsing in the hundreds outside of medical tents, shaking from fever, cold, or exhaustion. Now, does that accord with your recollection of events, this report coming from Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I have an entirely different opinion, and if you wish I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I may, I'll just take you through the various short passages of this report and it may be more convenient and more economic in our use of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Prendergast can turn over to the next page. The overall situation -- further up. Headed "Overall situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The refugees --" this report says -- "cannot leave the border area or receive assistance there. An OSCE representative told [the organisation] -" that's PHR, Physicians for Human Rights - "that the Macedonian government was resisting taking in the refugees until other countries agreed to provide refuge to them." Is it right that at that stage, March turning to April, your government was resisting taking refugees?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I reply? You see, the crowds in front of the tents mentioned in the first text, let me tell you something about that. When you place a large number of people in a limited area, that would normally lead to creation of crowds. But that doesn't mean that they were waiting in line in front of the tent for medical assistance or that medical assistance was denied to them. I assure you that medical assistance was provided to each and every person, and we continue to do that to this day. I told you that we still have refugees, Roma people, Macedonians and others, and it is not true that Macedonia denied them medical assistance. If you remember, there used to be a deputy or foreign minister in charge of refugees. He later became president, and he gave this statement. I think he said if you think that this assistance is not enough, maybe we should stop it altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further down the page, please, Mr. Prendergast, at the end of the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says this, middle of the page: "... once they'd crossed to the Macedonian side, international humanitarian agencies were not allowed by police to enter the 'no man's land' to provide aid for them. Some assistance was being provided by local Red Cross workers around the clock, but they were overwhelmed by the extent of the need." Now, that's the way this has been characterised by this human rights medical organisation. Do you agree with the way it is described?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot comprehend a text like this let alone say that I agree with what is stated here, because we indeed provided assistance to everyone who requested it. You know what the Red Cross teams are like and what the emergency medical teams are like. These are professionals who do their job, and there are many of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page --

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is really shameful that I have to listen to statements of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Medical Conditions. Despite the huge numbers of people in distress and suffering from serious medical conditions, medical aid was almost non-existent. Getting access to the medical tent is itself technically difficult for the population. Sick people had to cross out of the valley of mud and grass and pass police in riot gear in order to reach an emergency tent. Police sometimes refused to let sick persons pass. When they did allow passage, it was frequently only for the ill person, causing separation of family members. Another medical aid tent was placed amid the refugees in far reaches of the muddy field." Does that description accord with your recollection, please, Dr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this pertain perhaps to Stenkovac 1 and 2 camps or to the camp at the border? If this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the border, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just coming to ask you to clarify that. Are we talking about the same time and the same place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the border camp, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say about that, Dr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a lot to say, because this insults me and my state. It is not typical for us to deny medical assistance to someone, and we as professionals would never do it. The police was a bit further away from our tent and from other tents which were later set up by humanitarian organisations. These people had free access to us. There was no hindrance at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will find the geographical location identified on the first page, towards the bottom, where it says that they spent "... the day with medical workers and among tens of thousands of Albanian refugees in the 'no-man's land' between Kosovo and Macedonia at Blace." And as I indicated, the map shows that Blace is to the east of the border itself, and you can see that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, page number 16. It's page 16, and it's 26-W, where you can see the Djeneral Jankovic crossing and then you can see Blace to the east of that. Mr. Prendergast, if we could go to the last page -- second to last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find this. Mr. Nice says on page 16, whereas this entire document has five pages. So what is he referring to exactly? Oh, he's speaking about the atlas. I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can return to the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Access to refugees was described by this body in this way: "Access to the refugees is severely restricted. This is partly due to the Macedonian police, who have set up check points on the way to the border and prevent journalists and sometimes aid workers from getting in. PHR's physician-investigator was stopped at the border two days ago by police and, after providing identification, was told, 'There are enough doctors in there.' He was allowed to enter but only after the invitation from a physician inside. Representatives of the local Albanian refugee agency also told PHR that they had experienced difficulty in obtaining permission to provide assistance to the refugees." Were there difficulties put in the way of those seeking to help the refugees?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with this. I've already stated, and I can repeat, that this is offensive for my country and for me as a doctor. Our policemen, our soldiers, were brought up in such a way as to never deny an assistance to somebody who needed it. The same applies to doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question on this report: You didn't recall Physicians for Human Rights. You did recall Medecins sans Frontieres. Can you point to any reason, do you know of any reason why an organisation like Physicians for Human Rights could get its reporting so wrong?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd better ask them. I don't know how they could publish something like this. I disagree with this, and I would like to confront this colleague of mine and discuss it. I don't understand. We were present there. We walked around, and I told you that many photographs were rigged, set up, and there were things like that, but I disagree with what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next report, which I can take quite shortly, is the 9th of April, again quite early, having been released by the US State Department on the 7th of April. And it comes from the ambassador at large for war crimes, David Scheffer, who visited a large -- visited Blace, Macedonia, and interviewed a large number of Kosovo refugees. Dr. Aleksovski, the first paragraph of this report suggests that the ambassador visited Blace on three occasions, including during the night of April 1st and 2nd, and was able to interview refugees at length for a total of 15 hours without disclosing his identity but being free to move through the Blace camp, interviewing an estimated 200 refugees. First, were you aware at the time personally of any -- of this visit by American Ambassador Scheffer?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He -- we can go to the foot of the first page and I can deal with this report briefly in light of the witness's earlier evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ambassador says that by the date of his visit, April the 1st to the 2nd: " ... there was remarkable consistency in the refugees' accounts. Of course, because of the actions of Serb forces in Kosovo, these accounts cannot be individually verified at the present time. But the large and growing number of consistent reports by the refugees is too significant either to ignore or to understate. Kosovars are fleeing Kosovo not because of the NATO bombing campaign but because of the Serb assault on the civilian population." Pausing there, do you accept that by April the 1st or 2nd the complaints made were not of the NATO bombing campaign but of assaults by Serb forces on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already said that in the beginning they complained of the bombs falling, NATO bombs. And then later on as those stage managed, every one of them to the last one said that they had been fired at by the army and the police. I was there. Therefore, I cannot accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you're actually agreeing with me, but what I wanted to know was, and I'm not interested in your stage managed, I'm just interested in the change of account and the dates. Did this change of account that you referred to occur by about the 1st or 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've stated that too. When they transferred to Stenkovac 1 and 2, which was on the 5th and 6th, their accounts changed for the most part, and after that every single one stated that they had been forcibly expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you're following the point, Dr. Aleksovski. It's probably my fault. But this report from Ambassador Scheffer is built on his visit of the 1st and 2nd of April. We've looked at the way he opens his report, and although I'm not going to go through it, if Mr. Prendergast --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter. I don't think it's a report by him. It's compiled by someone called Dr. S. D. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the page that's on the screen at the moment, although I'm not going to go through it in detail, the visit by Ambassador Scheffer on the 1st and 2nd of April had the refugees giving consistent accounts of being told, "Go to NATO. Let NATO house you," or being deprived of their cash and identity documents, of being forced out of their homes, being told that they leave or die, being beaten, and being force marched and put on trains. Now, all I want to know from you, Dr. Aleksovski, is were those accounts being given by the 1st and 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're making me repeat what I've already stated. I told you that on the 1st, we started -- and after the 1st we started hearing an increasing number of accounts referring to the army and the police. And later on, everything we saw in those people, the injuries and their medical condition, that was not consistent with their accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third document, please, is the report or statement from the High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mary Robinson, dated the 6th of May, 1999. And we're moving on, Dr. Aleksovski. Very briefly this: Mary Robinson visited the region and visited, as we can see on the first page in the second paragraph, she visited Blace. Do you remember her visit?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I know that she was in Skopje, but I don't remember her visiting Blace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blace. I'm sorry. Were you working in the camps in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May of 1999, yes, I worked there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of passages from this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you can help us with this. This is again compiled by Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you tell us if this is a newspaper article or is it a report done by Ms. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights website.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you get it from this Mr. Stein's website, not from the UN website?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from Mr. Stein's website. It's identified as coming from the High Commissioner's website. It couldn't be located on the High Commissioner's website.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I'm afraid I can't help you with. But I can find out and I will help with you it. The material was located because of its connection with the expected evidence of this witness, but we'll find out a little bit more about Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, Dr. Aleksovski, Mrs. Robinson -- Mary Robinson visited Macedonia and Blace in May, according to this document - and we'll find out a little bit more about it - she said this -- the bottom of the first page. Thank you. "The full magnitude of the problem and its tragic consequences can only be realise when seen firsthand. Although I have been receiving reports from my field staff on the scale of the suffering being caused by this deliberate violation of human rights, I have been shocked and appalled at witnessing the actual plight of thousands of Kosovar Albanians forced from their homes." Now -- she then deals with those who didn't make it to the camps. By May of 1999, was the condition of the refugees in the camps such as to shock and appall a visitor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you describe the visit of Mrs. Robinson to Blace camp, and then you believe that what she saw there for an hour or two, no more than that, you would rather believe her account than our account, us who were there on a daily basis, who lived there, worked there, dealt with that every day. Naturally, when you see a large number of people in a small area, the impression cannot be a positive one. And yes, there was suffering there. Yes, there were injuries there. And this is something that I wouldn't wish upon any -- anyone, to have a large number of people in a small area. So naturally, for somebody visiting for an hour or two, the impression would be unpleasant. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- that's all I ask from that one. And the last document, which again is sourced directly from Stein but attributed to the UNHCR as a source, and I'll find out more about the routing of the material in a second, I hope, is a report by the High Commissioner for Human Rights, dated the 31st of May, said to be an advance and unedited version. I just look and see and ask your comment on these few observations. Do you remember the High Commissioner for Human Rights at the end of May reporting on the conditions generally of Kosovo refugees and dealing with the position in Macedonia to an extent?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there were reports, statements, all kinds of statements from different people, and I really can't put names to reports, or names and surnames, but there were many. And this last report, what I can say about that is that I remember that there were criticisms. There were praises too. But let me repeat: Please don't insult my country, because we really did everything that we could. We did the maximum we could and sometimes even to the disadvantage of our own citizens in order to give assistance and help to the refugees, both with respect to health protection and care and also with respect to other kinds of assistance and help, and that is why I really can't comment on reports like this. I know what we did. I know all the things that we undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksovski, it's only really for me to ask questions. You recurringly said please don't insult your country. I'm not insulting your country, I'm simply giving you an opportunity to comment on contemporaneous reporting that may be different from your evidence so that the Judges can have that in mind. I'm personally expressing no opinions, I'm only asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we could just look, please, Mr. Prendergast, at the second page of this report to see the -- from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're told that between -- or by this document that between the 2nd and 13th of May, the High Commissioner travelled to Macedonia, Albania, Bosnia and various other places so that the material was gathered in that first half of May. And if you'd go on, please, to the page, at the top, 4 of 16. A little further down. "The High Commissioner for Human Rights visited the Blace border crossing on the 2nd of May and spoke to some of the thousands of Kosovars waiting to be registered and granted permission to enter Macedonia. Several persons described how they had been compelled to leave their homes and all their possessions behind, either due to violence, threats, or the prevailing threatening atmosphere. In several cases males were separated from their families ... One victim showed a gunshot wound to his knee, while several others displayed fresh marks of beatings inflicted by Serbian police forces. Some refugees had spent weeks in the forest before leaving Kosovo." Now, this is, I repeat, the 2nd of May. Any reason to doubt first that such accounts would be given to the High Commissioner?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report describes the situation, some we have discussed, some aspects of it. Now, what he says here, the fresh situation, if it is -- fresh wounds, then fresh wounds would have to bleed. So I don't know about that, and I didn't understand what camp this refers to. So we recorded everything, but since you keep going back to this, you will see in the document that it was only later that injuries came to us. First of all, they hid their injuries and wounds because they were old injuries. So I don't know where the woman said this, what injuries she showed or whatever. But as to fresh marks, what I said was that our register reflected the truth. We recorded the truth. Now, what these people recorded, what these people filmed, if that woman had perhaps gone to a visitor without having asked for our help, I don't know why she would have done that, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few more references in this report and then I think I'm done. If you go on, please, Mr. Prendergast, to page 6 of 16. We come to torture and ill-treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Commissioner is reported to have interviewed refugees who had "experienced various forms of ill-treatment at the hands of Serbian paramilitary and police as well as of Yugoslav army soldiers. Various forms of ill-treatment have included beatings with fists and rifle butts, cruel treatment, rape and other forms of sexual assault, mutilation, shooting and threats of violence." And then this: "In Macedonia, the High Commissioner spoke with a refugee whose ear was mutilated by paramilitary forces ..." Now, it doesn't specify the location of this refugee there. It goes on, however, to say others reported to have physical abuse, including beatings with batons, being inflicted by Serbian authorities just before the refugees reached the border crossing at Blace. So it may be at Blace. Do your records contain anything about a refugee with a mutilated ear?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear about a case like that for the first time, and I don't think there would have been a case like that without coming to us and reporting to us, because at that time in Blace there was no team to -- which could have taken care of that. It would have needed hospital treatment, quite certainly, because it was the -- the auditor organ, the ear, and she would have come to us and so would the other people if they had been beaten and so on. So I told you about what we had seen, the work we had done, but that does not confirm this report or, rather, vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 10 of 16, please. And it's at the foot of the page under "Macedonia." "According to official government sources, Macedonia harbours more than 200.000 refugees from Kosovo. "Poor hygiene, lack of adequate medical attention and overcrowding of camps puts the health of refugees at risk. The lack of space is also affecting school programmes. The number of reported security incidents in the camps is low; in several cases, refugees have been arrested and taken away to local police stations for attempting to leave the camp without authorisation." Now, those are, I think, three or four aspects of the camps as at the first half of May. The first one was "lack of adequate medical attention and overcrowding puts the health of refugees at risk." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as giving health assistance and attention, I think that everything was done, of course, under the prevailing conditions. I know what it means when you come into a clinic, for example, when you have the state-of-the art equipment and everything, and it's quite a different thing when you give assistance in a tent. But given the prevailing conditions, we did what we could and gave sufficient medical attention and did what we could to help the people. Of course there were many cases -- even now, if you were to go to an outpatients department here in The Hague, you would see a different situation. You have hospitals, you have well-equipped clinics and so on. You can't organise that kind of thing under conditions in a tent. Now, as for the conflict with the police, I only remember that happening when there was a conflict between the Roma and the Albanian themselves, and then the police did have to intervene to separate the two groups, and the authorities were forced to separate the Roma from the Albanians. I know about that case. As to another conflict, other conflicts, other clashes, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With regard to this witness, the Chamber will appreciate I have simply been putting to him contemporaneous reporting. As to Dr. Stein, he is a lecturer in England. He has his own -- or he runs a website called Web Genocide Documents Centre, of which he is the director. These documents come from there. Whatever may be the status of these documents, if the Chamber would like them to be verified as coming from a different or more authoritative website, I will do my best to ensure that that is done. As to the documents themselves, obviously I would have preferred and would seek for them to be admitted into evidence. It's a matter for the Chamber. I realise that the practice to which the Chamber is inclining is that if the witness doesn't adopt something it may be that it's not going to be admitted. I don't want to keep arguing the same point. This material could be of value to the Chamber, but I'm comparatively neutral, having put the propositions from it, as to what happens to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just something in connection with what Mr. Nice asked for. I should like to draw your attention to the fact that the witness states quite clearly that it is not true what it says in this -- that what it says in these documents is not true, and I don't think that these documents can be introduced into evidence through this witness. The witness was there on the spot himself in an official capacity as head or director of the emergency service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We heard what he said, Mr. Milosevic. If you have just one or two questions, as I think would be appropriate in these circumstances, we could work for another five minutes. The witness could then leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Aleksovski, you mentioned in passing while you were saying how various footage or events were stage managed, that you saw allegedly people positioning somebody who was wounded in order to film that and then you saw this on television later on. Can you describe this event, this stage management of somebody who was allegedly wounded and how he was being positioned and how you came to the conclusion that he wasn't actually wounded.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the camp at the time, the Blace camp, and I described what happen. The cameras were placed in front of us, they called some people up, and this one man, one person walking quite normally went off with a cameraman, quite literally passed in front of our tent. He was taken off by the cameraman, and later on our team told me -- they came to me and said, "Director, we saw them positioning a perfectly healthy man and took footage, filmed him on crutches." And that evening I saw it televised over Macedonian television. We saw that same case, the same person, whereas he never came to us for help. We did not see that he was not able to walk or that he was in pain at all, and my conclusion was that that was all stage managed, and that's why I brought it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw the first -- you -- first of all you saw the man walking past your tent and later on you saw him filmed in pain on crutches. Is that what your explanation was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was on a stretcher, and that was televised by television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksovski, this first picture shows a fence, a barrier. On one side of the fence we can see policemen and on the other side we can see a group of refugees. Is that what you were telling us about, that the police for a time did not allow the people to leave the camp until the permanent camps, Stenkovac 1 and 2, were set up to accommodate them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true. They didn't allow them to pass because it would have been chaos in town if all these people had descended into town. So they were held back there until the camps were being prepared to accommodate them. Everybody knew about this, and of course that area there, there were large crowds of people, lots of people in a small space were kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this now: Did you have your own doctors teams on the other side of the fence or this side of the fence? That is to say, within that space, did you have your medical teams go within that space or were they outside that space and beyond the fence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were inside, towards the border crossing, and the police were on the other side, towards Skopje, on the other side of the barrier, so our teams were on one side, the police on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was no obstacle between the refugees and your medical teams offering and giving medical assistance if they were amongst the people and within the space that was set aside for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There were no obstacles. I absolutely deny that. And many times the policemen would come in if they needed anything, if they had a headache and wanted a tablet for their headache, or perhaps they had some stomach pains. We were there amongst the people and even the policemen would come and ask us for these tablets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some of these reports suggest that you did not succeed in giving aid and assistance to everyone. Were there any long queues and large crowds in front of your tent or was everybody who considered they needed medical assistance reach your tent and ask for medical help?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has been written down and I also said in -- there were 1.900 and some registered people. Some people came several times for help, either for tablets or for having some bandaged. But nobody was sent back by us. I ordered that everybody should be seen to. That was the position Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. taken by the Ministry of Health, that everybody should be helped. And I've already said, given the prevailing conditions, we did what we could. We gave basic assistance, and that was sufficient. Now, I read through all these reports and I can say that we took 22 women to hospital who gave birth. They were -- they delivered their babies in hospital. And I really can't say. And as to these reports, they're not correct, not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you already said they're not true and incorrect, and they are in contradiction with what you as an eyewitness saw. Take a look at this report by the High Commissioner for Human Rights, for instance, the one that was given you. It is dated the 31st of May 1999 and Mr. Nice drew our attention to page 6 of that report, page 6 of 16 pages, and it comes under the chapter of torture and ill-treatment, chapter D, or paragraph D, torture and ill-treatment. This is what it says in the middle of that first paragraph. It speaks about the person with the ear that was mutilated by the paramilitaries "and others reported to have physical abuse, "[In English] including beatings with batons being inflicted by Serbian authorities just before the refugees reached the border crossing at Blace." [Interpretation] That means beaten with batons just before they came into your territory where you gave assistance. Now, tell us this: Did you find a single Albanian with traces of beatings on their bodies, beatings with a blunt object, wooden object, not to say batons, but beaten and the traces of beatings? Did you have a single refugee with those kinds of wounds?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 32 years that I have been working in the emergency medical service, I have had ample opportunity of seeing people who were beaten with batons or blunt objects and everything else, and those kinds of cases comes to a -- come to us every day. Sometimes they are wounds from rifle butts and you can see it quite clearly when you're dealing with a wound of that kind. We know what batons are, what truncheons are, what rifle butts are and what kind of wounds and injuries they can inflict. And I can say quite certainly, and we would have no reason to deny this, that we had no reason to record cases of that kind because we never came across cases of that kind. I can't say that we ever had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean not a single case?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And here it says that they were beaten just before coming into your territory from Blace, at the Blace crossing. Would you have noticed injuries of that kind had they existed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had conditions of that kind existed, those people would certainly have come to us for assistance. They had no nobody else to come to but us, and we would quite certainly have seen traces of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now we go on to page 4 of that same document. This is what it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a minute. You say that they wouldn't have had anybody else to go to for assistance. Were there other human rights bodies there, the Red Cross or other agencies, offering help apart from your medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first days, no, there was no one else. They arrived later. But as I said before, the International Red Cross was unable to deal with such cases. Their staff was -- consisted of beginners, young doctors. Serious injuries had to be taken to the close hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did the other agencies to whom the refugees could have turned for help arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, around the 1st. Some of them came on the 30th, but on the 1st of April some of them arrived to the border, set up their tents, but they had nothing. They had no vehicles, they had no particular equipment, and even those people who initially went to them eventually turned to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are about seven, eight minutes beyond the break. Are you bringing your re-examination to a close now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am bringing it to a close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to determine when we should take the break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same to me. We can take the break now and then I will have a couple of more questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes. You must finish very quickly now so we can move on to your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksovski, in this document presented by Mr. Nice dated the 4th of April, 1999, "Medical group, witnessing public health crisis, condemns the refusal of Macedonia to accept Kosovo refugees," that's the document. I suppose you have the translation or you are receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have -- I don't have any interpretation. Does that mean I have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again in this document presented by Mr. Nice, this medical group testifying to health care issues, condemning the Macedonian government for their refusal to allow or, rather, extend assistance to Albanian refugees from Kosovo, urging immediate action by NATO, on page 2 it says "General Situation," and then it says: "The refugees cannot leave the border area --" You explained about that and we saw the footage or, rather, photographs, and then it says "or receive assistance there." Is it true that at the place where refugees were located inside the fence they were unable to receive assistance?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely inaccurate. They received both medical assistance, supplies, bread, everything at the border. They were not starving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say that what is written here is untrue.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it says: "... once they crossed to the Macedonian side [In English] international humanitarian agencies were not allowed by police to enter the 'no man's land' to provide aid for them. Some assistance was being provided by local Red Cross workers around the clock, but they were overwhelmed by extent of the need." [Interpretation] First of all, is it true that the Macedonian police did not allow humanitarian workers to come and extend assistance, whereas the latter were trying to come in?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely untrue. I know how the humanitarians worked. I know how our own Red Cross operated. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you were trying to give assistance to people but you did not manage to cover everyone who needed it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And you can see from the numbers of the work we performed, four medical teams were quite able to assist everyone who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there some people who were simply left waiting, whose turn never came because you couldn't -- you didn't have enough time or resources?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then on the next page we have a subtitle, "Medical conditions." It says: "[In English] Despite the huge numbers of people in distress and suffering from serious medical conditions, medical aid was almost non-existent." [Interpretation] Is this correct? So despite the huge numbers of people in distress, medical assistance was unavailable.

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, I am addressing you. You don't have to use re-examination for this purpose, because the witness has already clearly disagreed with all the propositions put forward by the Prosecutor in relation to this information. You don't have -- there's nothing to rehabilitate this witness on. He has already clearly disagreed, and we have taken note of that. You're now finished?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished, Mr. Robinson. I am bearing in mind that there were various international agencies present, and Mr. Nice stressed that the people who were the authors of this even won the Nobel Prize. They reflected the status of Albanian refugees quite incorrectly and inaccurately, and it has to be stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... against that is the witness's testimony that these reports constitute an affront to his country. The Chamber takes note of all of those bits and pieces of evidence. But I think we have spent a long time with this witness, and he need not have been here for this length of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask the witness if it's true what it says on page 4 about access to refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] Representatives of the local Albanian refugee agency also told PHR that it had also experienced difficulty in obtaining permission to provide assistance to the refugees." [Interpretation] Is it true that some Albanian medical staff tried to assist the refugees and you didn't let them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRE ALEKSOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such humanitarian organisations, but I -- let me say again, there was not a single humanitarian organisation who was there, willing to help, and we didn't let them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're finished. Thanks. I was just going to say that the Chamber considered the admissibility of these documents, and we are not admitting any of the documents apart from the three photographs which speak for themselves. We admit the three photographs minus the comments at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski, that constitutes your testimony at the Tribunal. Thanks for coming to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two of the documents that came from the site of Dr. Stein have now been sourced to their original prime sites. The one -- that's the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nice. Whether the witness has left the original tab 1, whether he can leave that to the Tribunal or not. We have to find that out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they verified it's an original. I told you, our documents are designated for permanent filing. Anybody from our service can use the documents. Anybody who wants to use them can make copies, but I don't think I can leave the original with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Take the original with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the impression that there is a slight misunderstanding here. Can I just ask Dr. Aleksovski if he could let us have the original for a while so that it can be compared to the copy, after which we would return it. Maybe not today, after a delay, that you need to examine the original and compare it to the photocopies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Judges have any doubts as to the original or the photocopies, I can leave the original for a while, but sooner or later I have to bring it back. It belongs to the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the original then will, as I indicated earlier, be exhibited along with the tabs 1 and 2. They'll be under seal, and we will return the original as soon as possible, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is at all possible, I would really have to take it with me. It doesn't take long to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You keep offering to let us have it and then changing your mind. Could you make your mind up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide it to you. I just don't understand how long you need it for, because I need to travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Registry is able to make a photocopy of it very promptly. There's no problem for you to take it back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, then. I think we understand each other now. So you may leave, and the original will be passed on to you after it has been copied. Arrangements will be made with the court deputy for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, in response to Judge Kwon's sharp eyes and concern, the documents of Dr. Stein have been sourced as to two of them, the report of Ambassador Scheffer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness may leave. I just want to make sure he understands that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may carry on, making use of time. And the 5th of May document about Mary Robinson have been sourced respectively to the State Department and United Nations web sites. The third one, the 1st of June advanced, unedited report has not yet been sourced to either of the two web sites, either UNHCR or HCHR -- or OHCHR. It may be the fact that there are two sites is one of the problems. Although it hasn't been sourced I can simply inform you that it is referred to in a BBC production I think for the same day as a report that was issued on that day, and it's also referred to in another government site. We'll carry on trying to find the original, but so far as we can see, it's a fair reflection of a report that was made even if we can't get it off the UN website.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it really makes no sense for Mr. Nice -- it's really inappropriate for Mr. Nice to offer reports by an American ambassador at a time -- from the time when this ambassador's country was bombing Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I stopped you because the comment is inappropriate. We have dealt with the matter. Your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While we are just waiting for the witness, who obviously has to be brought here, just an administrative matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him call the witness. Before you call the witness, Judge Bonomy will give the Chamber's ruling on those documents which the Prosecutor sought to produce through the witness Balevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are six items that the Chamber had to deal with, and we deny admission to three of them. Those are the document about the membership of Sloboda, the interview of Solevic quoted in Borba, and the extract from the Independent newspaper of September 1998 dealing with the rally at Nis. And we exhibit the clip of the video relating to the meeting on the 27th of April, 1987 - that's the meeting with the Kosovo Serbs - the extract from the book by Raif Dizdarevic, and the video clip showing the crowd at Gazimestan singing the Serbian anthem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Bonomy. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just a quick matter. I've been asked by the Registrar to arrange an ex parte hearing before the Trial Chamber for 8.00 tomorrow. If that could be arranged with your legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would have wished to be told to -- to what end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the matter concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know the matter that it concerns, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will be productive. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning at 8.00. Tomorrow morning at 8.00. Yes. It will be ex parte.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We did have a procedure whereby, although ex parte, you had indicated that you wouldn't object to the accused coming if he wished to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter doesn't -- the accused has shown no interest in the matter so it doesn't concern him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's not a matter for the Prosecution either, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Prosecution attended on the last occasion at the invitation or the permission of the parties or the Court, I draw to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You will be receiving a filing later on today so that you're fully briefed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, then. 8.00 tomorrow morning. Exhibit numbers for the last set of the Balevic documents. Three.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it will run from 830 to 31, 32, 832.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as for the video clip, we admit it. The Chamber noted some insufficient translation but which were corrected during the testimony. That's why we admit it without any reservation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now your next witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Mirko Babik. Babik is my next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your schedule says Goran Stojcik is your next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying this error in the schedule is of no particular significance, because we are dealing with three witnesses; Dr. Aleksovski, Stojcik, and Babik, all of them employed by the emergency medical centre, and their testimony is complementary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Call the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm calling Goran Stojcik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojcik.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to be time efficient, I will cover several issues very quickly. I note the time. Is it true that you completed your elementary school and secondary school in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you work presently and in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I currently work in the emergency medical service in Skopje as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are the driver of the emergency medical team?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes, the ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you work in that capacity in Skopje during the NATO aggression on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the entire time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the entire time of the NATO aggression in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you also on duty at a border crossing during that time; and if so, at which one? Were you also on duty in holding centres or camps; and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I was present at the official border crossing in Donje Blace as well as in Stenkovac 1 and Stenkovac 2 camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojcik, we have a map here showing this part of Macedonia. Would you please put it on the ELMO. The copy I have is better. Please take a pointer and show us the Donje Blace border crossing, the one that you were present at. Where was Stenkovac 1 and 2 camps located, and how far from Skopje? You can find Skopje up in the northern section.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Well, right here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the ELMO. Use your pointer, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here is where the official border crossing called Donje Blace is located. This is some 23 or 24 kilometres from the capital, Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were camps Stenkovac 1 and 2 located?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: They were located six and a half kilometres from Skopje. They were some 500 metres from each other, in the directions of Blace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please show us Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Tetovo is some 40 kilometres from Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to get to Tetovo, one must pass through Skopje.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Well, actually, going from the border to Skopje one must pass through Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You can now remove it from the ELMO because you have shown us everything we needed to see. So you covered that route regularly. You were on duty at the border crossing as well as both camps, Stenkovac 1 and 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were somebody who was on the ground, and as such you met with numerous Albanians who crossed into Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that entire time that you spent there, did you see a single Albanian who had arrived from Kosovo injured?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone who had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a single Albanian who had wounds inflicted by firearms or cold weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any foreign reporters, TV cameras, cameramen present at the border crossings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which TV crews were present, because you were there regularly. Were they near you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. They were very near our tents. And in the beginning of the NATO aggression on Yugoslavia, we immediately set up two tents at the official border crossing in Donje Blace. The camera crews were very near us. I think that these were crews from Turkey, Italy, BBC crews, CNN, many others. I can't enumerate them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, please, did you follow what was taking place there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. While I was there at work, I did follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they film Albanians regardless of their age or were they selective in their approach?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: There was some selective filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "selective filming"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: When I say "selective filming," I mean that the children and the elderly were set apart and filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they did some things that were inappropriate for TV crews, what is it that you saw them doing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Well, I was present there when an elderly man, some 65 years old, crossed the border crossing in Donje Blace. He had two children he held by the hand. And he came to the TV reporter who was there with his camera crew. They talked to the old man, and then the old man and the children retreated back some 50 metres and then re-entered but in a different light. The children cried loudly, screamed. It was an unimaginable sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And these members of the TV crew, did they explain to the refugees what they needed to do in front of the cameras?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. Before this scene was recorded, they had talked to them and stage managed the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where were these TV crews from, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a renowned Western TV outlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I would rather not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why would you rather not answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you must answer. There's no legal reason for you not to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well. I will tell you. The CNN was the most prominent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what way was it the most prominent?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Well, in stage managing, in setting up things that were to be filmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I would like to know is which organisation stage managed the particular incident which you've just described with the elderly gentleman and the two children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which TV crew stage managed that scene with the elderly man, the one that made the man re-enter with children crying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I said clearly that that was CNN. CNN TV outlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other examples where it was obvious that the scene was prepared for the filming and where the participants were coached or given suggestions as to what they should do? Can you describe anything else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. I can describe an event which outraged me. In Blace, there was a holding centre on the left side, and people were gathering there between the highway and the Lepenac River. That was in the first days. I remember that they took a child and threw the child into the mud and then TV crews ran to the site and filmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when the child was thrown into mud, it cried?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes, quite a lot, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other cases where the refugees were made to repeat the scene?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I was an eyewitness only in this case that I've already described to you. And as for others, I've heard things from my colleagues, and I can tell you about that if the Court will allow that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any need for the witness to state what he has heard from his colleagues, because the two cases that he described were the cases that he was an eyewitness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a matter for you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have another case that you can quote that would be quite interesting in relation to the stage managing of the behaviour of refugees?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. I know of another case which took place in the camps when the camps, Stenkovac 1 and 2, were set up. There was a group of young men, quite a lot of them, who took our ambulances without our permission, and they would go to the tents where a young man was moaning and was all bended down as though he had been injured. The TV crews came and filmed that, and as soon as the filming was over and the crews left, the young man jumped from the stretchers and all of them were quite happy and celebrating this event, and then they returned the stretchers back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was enough. Now, please tell us something about the behaviour of Albanian refugees in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I just ask him a question about that. That was a scene that you witnessed yourself? No? It was a scene of which you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I just told you now is something I heard from my colleagues, whereas the first two cases that I told you first about were the cases that I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you witnessed these scenes which were staged, did you do anything? Did you say anything to the -- to those refugees who were -- who were acting out parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, I would like to say that I was there in humanitarian capacity, providing assistance to the refugees. I had no authority to get into any discussion with them or to utter any comments. With all those security forces present, I don't think it would have been appropriate for a member of a medical team to say something or comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the behaviour of the Albanian refugees from Kosovo in Skopje? What was their conduct like there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Some of them came from rural areas, some came from urban areas. Those who had money initially were transferred into the city. They had relatives in Skopje. Some of them rented out rooms, some went to hotels, depending on how much money they had. And I can tell you openly that they had a good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that there were enough of them who had sufficient money to put themselves up in hotels and to go around town and act like any other citizens would; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to observe whether they had IDs on them, money, mobile phones, weapons, or anything else, anything else you noticed and would like to tell us about now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Well, as I saw the situation when I was present, I could see that those who were in the camps had money because they bought cigarettes. Taxis -- taxi drivers from Skopje would bring cigarettes for them every day. Later on, kiosks were set up where they could buy things. As for mobile phones, I can tell you that some individuals had two or three mobile phones on them. There were some who were dressed quite well, I could even say extravagantly dressed. There were young people there with Walkmans and pets. As for documents, I couldn't say anything, because all those who came to seek medical assistance in our infirmaries and so on, this is something that our medical staff can tell you more about because they have everything recorded in medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see or do you know whether any of them were armed? Did you see any such cases?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among those refugees from Kosovo, in addition to Albanians, there were also the Roma there. Did you see the Roma there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOJCIK
utterances.text: Yes. There were many of them. But from the border crossing, from the very border crossing, the Roma would go to a different area because there was some animosity from the very beginning there. The food that was distributed would be given to Albanians to distribute among themselves, and then one Roma man came, and I don't know how he managed to come out, but he came and complained about the fact that the food did not reach them at all. The animosity escalated to such a level that in Stenkovac, somebody was almost lynched. And were it not for security forces and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
